Abstract
We estimate the net primary productivity (NPP) based on bio-argo measurements using three algorithms: Vertically 
Generalised Production Model (VGPM), Eppley-VGPM and the original Carbon-based Production Model (CbPM). To do 
this, we made a dataset of Chlorophyll-a (Chl-a), temperature, and salinity from argo measurements and then computed 
the NPP for the north Indian Ocean (NIO, 5° S–25° N, 40°–100° E). These new data are compared with satellite-based NPP, 
and the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) suggests a better performance of argo-based standard VGPM with an RMSE of 
0.20 g C ­m−2 ­day−1. We have calculated the bias for two seasons: winter (December, January and February: DJF) and sum-
mer (June, July, August and September, JJAS), which are characterised with high productivity in NIO. The bias is smaller 
for standard VGPM and Eppley-based VGPM, in which the former has a bias of − 0.1 g C ­m−2 ­day−1 in DJF and − 0.08 g C 
­m−2 ­day−1 in JJAS. The correlation between satellite and argo-based VGPM is 0.33, suggesting that this is the best among 
the estimates and can be used for NPP studies in NIO. Furthermore, the individual argo-based NPP of the Arabian Sea 
(AS, 5°–25° N, 50°–75° E), Bay of Bengal (BoB, 6°–18° N, 76°–95° E) and Equatorial Indian Ocean (Eq IO, 5° S–5° N, 60–90° 
E) is tightly related to wind stress (WS), mixed layer depth (MLD) in AS and BoB.
Keywords  Bio-argo · NPP data · VGPM · Eppley-VGPM · CbPM
1  Introduction
Marine Net Primary Productivity (NPP) or oceanic NPP is the difference in the amount of carbon produced by photosyn-
thesis and respiration of phytoplankton [1]. It is a key parameter to account for the ecosystem health and to monitor 
the spatio-temporal changes in biogeochemical cycles. NPP is estimated as a function of biomass and incident solar 
radiation [2]. Phytoplankton, the predominant autotrophs, undergo photosynthesis in the ocean’s sunlit zone, and is 
the primary component of NPP and food to organisms, constituting the fundamental structure of the marine food web.
Marine NPP has a major role in regulating the increasing levels of ­CO2 in the atmosphere [3]. The conversion of Dissolved 
Inorganic Carbon (DIC) into Organic Carbon (OC) that supports the marine food web largely controls carbon transfer into 
abyssal depths for longer periods. As atmospheric ­CO2 is steadily increasing over the north Indian Ocean (NIO), with an 
average trend of 2.12 ppm ­year−1 [4, 5], it is essential to study its impact on NPP, which affects the biological pump in NIO. 
The warming scenarios prevailing in the tropical oceans will likely stress NPP and marine ecosystems [6, 7] and can alter the

distribution of atmospheric ­CO2 [8]. Thus, studying NPP is imperative for understanding the perturbations in ocean biogeo-

The NIO consists of both the Bay of Bengal (BoB: 5°– 25° N, 76°–95° E) and Arabian Sea (AS: 5°–25° N, 50°–75° E). AS is 
located in the west and BoB in the east of the Indian subcontinent, which exhibit notable differences in their physical and 
biological characteristics, primarily driven by seasonal monsoonal forcing [9, 10]. The AS has two peaks of NPP: one in winter 
(December, January and February; DJF) due to the winter convection [11] the other in summer (June, July, August and Sep-
tember; JJAS) due to monsoonal upwelling [12]. AS exhibits a weaker stratification allowing more frequent vertical nutrient 
transport through wind-driven upwelling and deep winter mixing. BoB is traditionally considered as a low-productive basin 
due to strong stratification and riverine influx, but it shows a NPP peak in the southeast coast of Sri Lanka during JJAS [13].
Satellite measurements provide Chlorophyll-a (Chl-a), which is a proxy of phytoplankton, that has global coverage over a 
longer period, enabling the estimation of NPP [14]. Global coverage of shortwave infrared radiation (SWIR) around 685 nm 
aids in detecting phytoplankton fluorescence [15]. Due to their high spatial and temporal availability, satellite-based meas-
urements are used in calculating NPP [2]. Vertically Generalised Production Model (VGPM) is among the most widely used 
NPP data for understanding marine productivity and its drivers [16–18]. Kalita and Lotliker [19] analysed NPP using different 
satellite-based algorithms in NIO and found that models perform differently in different regions of NIO. Recently, satellite-
based data were constructed based on Ocean Color Climate Change Initiative (OC-CCI) Chl-a. This is a multi-sensor dataset 
by Ryan-Keogh et al. [20] and was compared to single sensor data based on MODerate Resolution Imaging Spectrometer 
(MODIS) measurements, and found that these multi-sensor data performed better than that of single sensor. Though the 
satellite-based studies provide larger spatial and temporal coverage, they often fail to represent the changes in biogeochem-
istry in cloud-covered and coastal areas. For instance, BoB is loaded with coloured dissolved organic matter (CDOM) and 
suspended matter contributed by the high riverine inputs, making it a complex basin in terms of its optical properties and 
reduced Chl-a retrieval accuracy [21]. Nevertheless, the satellite-based algorithms are also mostly based on global oceans 
and thus, the existing algorithms need to be regionally tuned to account for their optical properties for a better estimation 
of their biological features [22].
The first studies on NPP in NIO were mostly based on in-situ and ship-based measurements and were dedicated to a few 
days. For instance, Qasim [23] quantified NPP in the northern AS and found that the amount of NPP in the coastal areas of 
the eastern, western and northern AS was thrice that in the open ocean, as assessed using the measurements performed by 
oceanographic cruises of Indian Naval Ships Darshak and Gaveshana, and the International Indian Ocean Expedition during 
the monsoon season of 1974 and 1976. The Indian Joint Global Ocean Flux Studies reported NPP of 807 mg C ­m−2 ­day−1 at 
a station located at 21° N 68° E in the northern AS during JF of 1995 [11]. A high NPP of 220.7 mg C ­m−2 ­day−1 triggered in 
the vicinity of cold-core eddies was reported in BoB using on-board measurements in the summer of 2001 [24]. Girishkumar 
et al. [16] quantified the role of physical and biological processes using argo measurements during the cyclones Hudhud and 
Vardah in BoB. Though the in-situ measurements perform better than the satellite measurements for regional biogeochemical 
studies [25–27], they are not suitable for long-term studies related to trend detection due to their limited temporal coverage.
Some of the previous studies have attempted to use depth-wise Chl-a from bio-argo instead of satellite Chl-a measure-
ments in the available satellite-based algorithms in other basins. For instance, in-situ measurements are applied to estimate 
NPP in the western North Atlantic using a modified Carbon-based Production Model (CbPM; [28, 29]). The vertical structure 
of phytoplankton was obtained from bio-argo floats in the Southern Ocean using modified CbPM [30]. The study also dem-
onstrated the need for argo profiling data to improve the existing NPP algorithms.
Although both satellite and in-situ measurements have their own merits and limitations, their combined use is less 
explored for NIO. The argo-based estimates of NPP have not been attempted for NIO except for some cyclone-based studies 
[16]. The satellite-based algorithms, which are already used for estimating NPP, are mostly based on global ocean measure-
ments. The objective of this study is to construct NPP data using the available bio-argo measurements and is the first attempt 
to estimate the argo-based NPP based on VGPM, Eppley VGPM and CbPM using the in situ measurements. The main objec-
tives of the study are to prepare argo-based estimates of NPP based on existing satellite-based algorithms, and to evaluate 
the argo-based estimates against the satellite-based algorithms.

2  Data and methods
2.1  Ground‑based and satellite measurements
To make the argo-based estimates of NPP, we require continuous bio-argo measurements in NIO. This study uses 
the available bio-argo measurements obtained from the Institut Français de Recherche pour l’Exploitation de la Mer 
(IFREMER). The bio-argo floats are automatic profilers consisting of biogeochemical and conductivity–temperature 
depth sensors, facilitating good quality in-situ measurements at different temporal scales. Surface and subsurface 
measurements from these bio-argo floats help understand the state of biologically active regions of the oceans [16, 
31]. We use 51 float measurements taken during the period from 2013 to March 2024. Our analysis is for NIO (0–25° 
N, 40–100° E, Fig. 1) and we use temperature, salinity and Chl-a from the gridded data (1° resolution) made using the 
argo measurements. The wind stress data are taken from TropFlux, generated from the European Centre for Medium-
Range Weather Forecast Re-Analysis Interim (ERA-I) reanalysis [32]. Since these TropFlux data are also available in 
1° resolution, all datasets used for making the gridded NPP data are of the same native resolution, and thus, do not 
require further data matching process.
For constructing NPP data, we use the three existing satellite-based algorithms, and depthwise Chl-a and tem-
perature are used instead of the traditional satellite temperature and Chl-a. We compare the argo and satellite-based 
algorithms for uncertainty estimation. The satellite-based NPP algorithm data for the period 1998–2022 are obtained 
from Ryan-Keogh et al. [20]. We use three algorithms: Standard VGPM [2], Eppley-VGPM [33] and the original CbPM 
[34]. Standard and Eppley-VGPM estimate NPP from surface Chl-a using a temperature-dependent function of Chl-a 
based on photosynthetic efficiency. Standard VGPM calculates NPP as a function of Chl-a, incident light and photo-
synthetic efficiency. The only difference between Eppley and standard VGPM is in the calculation of temperature-
dependent photosynthetic efficiency, which is a seventh-order polynomial in the standard VGPM, whereas an expo-
nential function of temperature is adopted in the former. The Eppley-based VGPM used for NPP estimation is based 
on Morel [35]. The euphotic depth (Zeu) is calculated based on Morel and Berthon [36]. More details on VGPM can be 
found in Eppley [33], Behrenfeld and Falkowski [2] and Saba et al. [37]. The third algorithm used to estimate NPP is 
the original CbPM, which is based on carbon and uses particulate backscattering coefficients for estimating carbon 
concentration [34]. The backscattering coefficient (bbp) at 443 nm used in the estimation of carbon to chlorophyll 
ratio (described in methods) is taken from MODIS at a horizontal resolution of 4 × 4 km.

The annual cycle of NPP is analysed using the argo and satellite-based estimates of NPP using all three algorithms. 
The argo-based VGPM reproduces the seasonal cycle in AS and moderately well in BoB. The seasonal cycles in BoB are 
better reproduced by argo estimates of Eppley VGPM than standard VGPM. CbPM-based estimates do not reproduce

The scatter diagram of argo and satellite-based estimates of NPP (Fig. 3) reveal a strong positive correlation and the best 
agreement among the estimates for NIO. Eppley-based VGPM shows a positive correlation and reasonable agreement 
with the satellite-based estimates. On the other hand, as evident from the seasonal cycle, the CbPM argo-based NPP 
estimates exhibit a poor agreement with those of satellite-based, than those of standard VGPM and Eppley-VGPM. The 
correlation coefficient ­(R2) values (shown in Fig. 3) reveal that the VGPM algorithm outperforms the other two for NIO. 
To better assess the performance of argo-based estimates of NPP, we have also conducted a paired t-test among the 
argo-based algorithms and the results are summarised in Table S2. These results show that all three estimates of NPP 
using argo inputs differ significantly from one another, indicating that they are not interchangeable and each algorithm 
brings its own bias or structural difference in estimating NPP.
3.2  Skill assessment of Argo and satellite‑based NPP
We have also quantitatively estimated the bias, RMSE, MAPE, and correlation to assess the skill of argo-based NPP com-
pared to satellite-based NPP. We have converted the satellite and argo-based NPP to g C ­m−2 ­day−1 and estimated the 
bias, MAPE, RMSE and found the correlation. The bias is calculated for the two seasons of DJF and JJAS, which are char-
acterised by higher NPP (Fig. 4). Bias is smaller for standard VGPM and Eppley-based VGPM. VGPM exhibits a smaller bias 
of − 0.1 g C ­m−2 ­day−1 in DJF and − 0.08 g C ­m−2 ­day−1 in JJAS. Eppley-based estimates also exhibit similar values of NPP 
as those of VGPM.
The MAPE of NPP estimates give an accurate measure of relative percentage error with closer to zero values, giving 
more accurate estimates. The MAPE values are 0.4 for VGPM and 0.62 for Eppley-VGPM. The RMSE values provide an esti-
mate of errors, with values closer to zero indicating smaller errors. The RMSE is the smallest for VGPM (0.20 g C ­m−2 ­day−1), 
followed by Eppley-VGPM (0.27 g C ­m−2 ­day−1), and thus, these two estimates are reliable for studying NPP in NIO. The

3.3  Interannual variability of NPP and causative mechanisms
We also examine the interannual variability of NPP using the newly constructed data. Figure 6 shows the interannual 
variability of standard VGPM NPP, Curl of WS and MLD in AS, BoB and Eq IO. We have chosen curl of WS and MLD to iden-
tify the causative factors responsible for the biogeochemical processes there. We consider standard VGPM NPP here, 
based on the performance assessed in the previous section. High wind stress curl values are observed in AS in JJAS due 
to strong winds during monsoon, which induce upwelling in AS. These contribute to higher NPP, as observed in NPP 
variability. For instance, in mid-2015 and 2017, there were periods of positive wind stress curl, consistent with the higher 
NPP in AS. High WS curl corresponds to upwelling, which is the dominant mechanism responsible for higher produc-
tivity in AS during JJAS [10]. In contrast, negative WS curl corresponds to downwelling [42], which pushes the surface 
waters downwards, often reducing surface nutrient levels. The curl of WS exhibits significant variations in BoB and Eq IO 
with intermittent positive and negative values. The positive values of WS curl correspond to higher NPP in both basins, 
although the values of NPP are not as high as in AS.
Deeper MLD contributes to higher NPP in AS during JF and JJAS [43]. The newly constructed argo-based NPP rep-
resents the dynamical processes prevailing in AS. MLD was close to 100 m in early 2014, corresponding to higher NPP 
around the same period. This was also concurrent with the low surface temperature observed in 2014. Similarly, the high 
MLD and WS, observed in 2015 can be attributed to the passage of cyclones Chapala (2015) and Megh (2015) in AS. The 
passage of these cyclones enhanced Chl-a and NPP significantly from the pre-cyclone values [17]. The high (low) wind 
stress in BoB is also associated with deep (shallow) MLD. NPP in BoB does not reveal any substantial variability. The higher 
NPP observed in Eq IO is also consistent with the deep MLD (100 m) in October–December in 2017 and JJAS in 2018. The 
observed SST fluctuations exhibit the observed seasonal fluctuations observed in AS, BoB and Eq IO, making the newly 
constructed argo-data suitable for long-term and short-term studies in NIO. The physical and biogeochemical processes

4  Discussion
The newly constructed data have good agreement with other independent measurements and they well reproduce the 
seasonal and annual cycles. For instance, we have tested reliability of the data to reproduce the stability of the water 
column by computing ­N2. The data reproduces the seasonal variability of ­N2. In addition, we also analyse the temperature 
and Chl-a in AS, BoB and Eq IO to ensure the reliability of data. In general, there are two temperature peaks in AS and BoB, 
one in March–April and the other in October. The primary peak has a value of around 30 °C and close to 28 °C during the 
second peak, but above 30 °C in BoB during both peaks. The AS is characterised by deeper MLD, which is greater than 
60 m in DJF and JJAS. BoB is featured with a shallow MLD (30–40 m) in JJAS. The high river influx makes BoB stratified, 
and thus the shallower MLD [9]. We analyse the depth-wise temperature in these regions to ensure that the gridded data 
are reliable for the estimation of NPP. MLD is deeper in Eq IO (~ 50 m) in JJAS, and October and November (ON) and gets 
shallower (~ 30 m) by DJF and MAM. The Eq IO is characterised by higher temperatures during the equinoxes (21 March 
and 21 September), which are when the equatorial regions receive the maximum solar radiation.
The strong seasonality in the gridded argo data could be attributed to the number of profiles, and spatial and temporal 
coverages of the profiles used for the creation of the data. The difference between gridded argo and satellite Chl-a in BoB 
is about 0.2 mg ­m−3. The gridded argo data depict smaller values of Chl-a. The satellite data depict higher values of Chl-a 
during July–August, whereas the argo Chl-a does not exhibit much seasonal variation. The argo measurements capture 
the seasonal signatures of upwelling based on cooler temperatures and lower ­N2 values, as observed in Figure S3 and 
S4 for AS. Among the three regions, a clear seasonal cycle of temperature, ­N2 and Chl-a is observed in AS. The depth of 
SCM shifts towards the surface in August and to 20 m in January due to the upwelling driven by monsoonal currents 
[12] and winter convection mixing [11]. In other months, the depth of SCM is close to 50 m in AS (Figure S5). Chl-a in 
BoB is typically smaller in magnitude compared to that in AS as they are more stratified, where the winds are not strong 
enough to break the stratification prevailing in BoB [46].
In monsoon-dominated regions like NIO, it is not necessary that a single algorithm performs well for the entire NIO. We 
assess the annual and seasonal variability of Chl-a based (VGPM and Eppley-VGPM) and carbon-based (CbPM) algorithms. 
Previous studies have shown that these algorithms perform differently in different provinces of NIO [19]. For instance, 
VGPM effectively captures the bimodal peaks in AS during the summer and winter monsoons, where nutrient-driven 
productivity dominates. This is particularly important because the monsoon-driven upwelling is not tightly related 
to SST. It also effectively captures the phytoplankton responses to the rapid nutrient pulses and mixed layer shoaling

is better for AS, unlike Eppley VGPM, which reveals a temperature-dependent relationship. On the other hand, Eppley-
VGPM underperforms in monsoon-dominated areas and fails to accurately represent the bloom intensities [19]. Nev-
ertheless, BoB, which has highly stratified waters and optical interference, CbPM underperforms because they rely on 
optical backscattering or light-attenuation coefficients. Despite using the fixed ­Pbopt approach in VGPM, it outperforms 
the other two algorithms, probably due to its relatively simplified approach for estimation of NPP. Besides this, the ­Pbopt 
calculation [47] also accounts for the equatorial and tropical waters, as in NIO.
Given the physical and biological characteristics of NIO, satellite-based estimates of NPP often have many limitations 
[19]. The presence of cloud cover, optical interference and vertical stratification, particularly in BoB, obscures surface sig-
nals and prevents the detection of subsurface chlorophyll maxima that can substantially contribute to total productivity 
[48]. Incorporating argo-based data into satellite model validation and regional productivity assessments is essential for 
improving NPP estimates and better understanding the region’s response to monsoon forcing and climate variability. 
The satellite-based NPP estimates are generally used for long-term studies of NPP due to their large spatial and temporal 
coverage. However, satellite-based estimates are primarily based on surface dynamics and have assumptions on the 
subsurface processes, whereas in a biologically active region such as NIO, the mixing and entrainment processes play a 
greater role in biogeochemistry. Furthermore, the satellite-based estimates are designed for global oceans, whereas the 
argo-based estimates are based on the available floats in NIO.
The lower bias and error statistics found for standard VGPM and Eppley-VGPM likely reflect their ability to better cap-
ture the surface-driven productivity patterns in NIO, where the monsoonal mixing and shallow mixed layers strongly 
regulate phytoplankton growth [19]. The relatively weak correlation with argo-based estimates highlights the limitations 
of satellite sensors in detecting subsurface productivity features such as the deep chlorophyll maxima, particularly in 
stratified regions like BoB. These discrepancies underscore the importance of integrating vertical structure such as MLD, 
­N2 and chlorophyll profiles into validation efforts to improve satellite-based NPP estimates [49].
Understanding the uncertainties and limitations of satellite-derived NPP estimates has important policy implications 
for regional ocean management, food security and climate adaptation strategies [50]. Accurate estimates of primary 
production are essential for assessing the health of marine ecosystems, forecasting fishery yields, and designing marine 
protected areas in the monsoon-driven NIO [51]. The demonstrated value of argo-based observations in capturing sub-
surface productivity reinforces the need for sustained investments in biogeochemical float programs and region-specific 
calibration of remote sensing algorithms. Incorporating such data into policy frameworks can improve the reliability of 
marine resource assessments and help coastal nations develop adaptive strategies in response to climate-driven changes 
in ocean productivity.
5  Conclusion
Bio-argo profiles are used to construct argo-based estimates of NPP in NIO by replacing the satellite Chl-a and SST in 
the existing algorithms with depth-wise Chl-a and temperature. These are further evaluated against the satellite-based 
NPP algorithms. Upon further investigation, it was found that standard VGPM outperforms the Eppley VGPM and CbPM 
in NIO with lower bias, RMSE and higher correlation with the satellite-based algorithms.

Abstract: We estimate the net primary productivity (NPP) based on bio-argo measurements using three algorithms: Vertically Generalised Production Model (VGPM), Eppley-VGPM and the original Carbon-based Production Model (CbPM). To do this, we made a dataset of Chlorophyll-a (Chl-a), temperature, and salinity from argo measurements and then computed the NPP for the north Indian Ocean (NIO, 5° S–25° N, 40°–100° E). These new data are compared with satellite-based NPP, and the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) suggests a better performance of argo-based standard VGPM with an RMSE of 0.20 g C ­m−2 ­day−1. We have calculated the bias for two seasons: winter (December, January and February: DJF) and sum- mer (June, July, August and September, JJAS), which are characterised with high productivity in NIO. The bias is smaller for standard VGPM and Eppley-based VGPM, in which the former has a bias of − 0.1 g C ­m−2 ­day−1 in DJF and − 0.08 g C ­m−2 ­day−1 in JJAS. The correlation between satellite and argo-based VGPM is 0.33, suggesting that this is the best among the estimates and can be used for NPP studies in NIO. Furthermore, the individual argo-based NPP of the Arabian Sea (AS, 5°–25° N, 50°–75° E), Bay of Bengal (BoB, 6°–18° N, 76°–95° E) and Equatorial Indian Ocean (Eq IO, 5° S–5° N, 60–90° E) is tightly related to wind stress (WS), mixed layer depth (MLD) in AS and BoB.
